title: No threat? Improve a piece before you spend a pawn move
outcomes: Names the threat a pawn move is meant to stop before playing it
Plays a useful piece move in positions where nothing needs preventing
Does not chase a well-placed piece with a pawn when the engine rates the chase clearly worse
Tells a real threat from a harmless pawn move by asking what happens if he gets a free move

steps.text: In **Defence by waiting: when it works** you learned to wait when he has no way forward. Now the move itself. When nothing needs preventing, the tempting spends are pawn moves: a rook pawn to stop a pin, a pawn to chase a piece that is well placed. Each one is a decision you cannot take back. Before any such move ask: **what exactly does this stop, and is that threat real?** If not, improve a piece.

steps.caption: Black would like to chase the bishop on f4 with a pawn.

line.say: The bishop simply takes the pawn.

claims.statement: g5 is at least 2 pawns worse than the engine's best move (depth 16).
Along the engine's best-defence line Black ends behind in material.

steps.text: Waiting is right while the position is equal or better and he has no real target; a pawn move that prevents nothing is lost time (a **rule of thumb**). It fails when the threat is real: then you must answer it. It also fails when he has a plan that, once begun, cannot be stopped later; that is the subject of **Prophylaxis: ask what he wants, then decide if it is real**, and this lesson does not test it.

steps.title: One position, three small changes
steps.prompt: White has just moved a piece. Predict for each: does the move threaten anything? Then check.
In your next game, the next time you want to play a rook pawn or chase a piece with a pawn, write down what the move stops. Afterwards: was that threat real?
